00Orientation

How this book works

Five parts: cloud foundations, running code, containers and delivery, operating in production, and Linux. Every service is shown on AWS and GCP side by side.

Ramu rents kitchens in a food court

Instead of building his own restaurant buildings, Ramu now rents kitchen space in giant food courts run by two landlords, Amazon and Google. He rents as many stoves as today's crowd needs and pays by the hour (the cloud). His recipes travel in sealed tiffin boxes that taste the same in any kitchen (containers). A floor manager decides which kitchen runs which tiffin and replaces any stove that breaks (Kubernetes). A conveyor belt from his test kitchen to every counter delivers new recipes safely (CI/CD).

How deep?

An SDE-2 interview won't ask you to recite every AWS service. It asks you to design and justify: "how would you deploy this service, make it highly available, secure it and know when it breaks?". Each chapter ends with that kind of question. The Spring Boot app we deploy in Chapter 14 is the one built in Spring Boot · Chapter 9.

Cloud foundations: regions, accounts, permissions and networks

Everything else in the cloud sits on four ideas: where things run (regions and zones), who may do what (IAM), how traffic flows (VPC), and who is responsible for what (shared responsibility).

Cloud basics: models, regions, responsibilityAWS and GCP: the service mapIAM: identities, roles and policiesVPC networking
01Foundations

Cloud basics: service models, regions and shared responsibility

The cloud is renting computing on demand, paid by use. The more managed the service, the less you operate and the less you control.

In the food court

Ramu can rent an empty kitchen shell and bring his own stoves and staff (IaaS), rent a fully equipped kitchen where he just cooks (PaaS), or simply order from another restaurant and resell (SaaS). The food court has several buildings in each city (availability zones) and branches in many cities (regions), so a fire in one building doesn't close him down.

Regions, availability zones and edge locations

region
A geographic area

e.g. ap-south-1 (Mumbai), asia-south1 (GCP Mumbai). Choose by latency to users, data-residency law and service availability. Data doesn't leave a region unless you send it.

availability zone
Isolated data centres in a region

Separate power, cooling and network, a few km apart, connected by low-latency links. Spread across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

edge location
Points of presence near users

Hundreds of sites used by CDNs (CloudFront, Cloud CDN) and DNS to serve content close to users.

Pricing modelHow it worksUse for
On-demandpay per second/hour, no commitmentspiky or unknown workloads
Savings Plans / Reserved / Committed usecommit 1–3 years for large discountssteady baseline load
Spot / Preemptible (Spot VMs)spare capacity at deep discounts, can be reclaimed with short noticebatch jobs, CI runners, stateless workers
Serverlesspay per request and execution timebursty, event-driven, low-traffic services
Lock it in

Empty shell, equipped kitchen, or just order in.

IaaS → PaaS → serverless → SaaS: less to operate, less control. Region = geography, AZ = isolated building; deploy across 2+ AZs. The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it.

Interview questions

What is the shared responsibility model?

The provider is responsible for security of the cloud (data centres, hardware, hypervisor, managed-service internals). The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: IAM, network rules, OS patching on VMs, application code, data encryption choices and configuration. The line moves toward the provider as you use more managed services.

How do you choose a region?

Latency to most users, legal/data-residency requirements (e.g. Indian payment data rules), availability of the services you need, price differences between regions, and a second region for disaster recovery if required.

AWS strengths

Largest service catalogue and market share, mature enterprise features, huge ecosystem and hiring pool.

GCP strengths

Global VPC and load balancer, GKE (Kubernetes came from Google), BigQuery, Cloud Run's simplicity, strong data/AI tooling.

Interview angle

Name the category first ("a managed queue"), then the service on the cloud they use. Avoid lock-in where it's cheap to (containers, Terraform, open protocols), accept it where it buys a lot (managed DBs).

Lock it in

Same facilities, different signboards.

EC2 ↔ Compute Engine, S3 ↔ GCS, RDS ↔ Cloud SQL, Lambda ↔ Cloud Run functions, Fargate ↔ Cloud Run, EKS ↔ GKE, SQS ↔ Pub/Sub.

Interview questions

A notable networking difference between AWS and GCP?

An AWS VPC is regional; connecting regions needs peering or Transit Gateway. A GCP VPC is global with regional subnets, so VMs in different regions share one private network, and GCP's external HTTP(S) load balancer has a single global anycast IP.

Next: IAM: identities, roles and policies →
03Foundations

IAM: who can do what to which resource

Every API call in the cloud is checked: which identity, which action, which resource, under which conditions. Grant the least privilege, prefer short-lived role credentials over long-lived keys.

In the food court

Staff don't get master keys. The baker's badge opens the oven room only, during his shift. A delivery partner gets a temporary pass valid for one hour. And the kitchen robot also has a badge (a role), so nobody tapes a key to it.

ConceptAWSGCP
Human identityIAM Identity Center (SSO) users, or IAM users (avoid)Google accounts / Workspace / Cloud Identity
Machine identityIAM role (assumed → temporary STS credentials)service account
PermissionsJSON policies attached to identities or resourcesroles (bundles of permissions) bound to principals on a resource
Pods → cloudEKS Pod Identity / IRSAGKE Workload Identity Federation
CI → cloud without keysOIDC federation (GitHub Actions → role)Workload Identity Federation
Org guardrailsOrganizations + SCPsOrganization policies
Do

Least privilege, scoped to resources. Roles/service accounts for workloads. SSO + MFA for humans. Separate accounts/projects per environment. Audit with CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs.

Don't

Use the root account. Put access keys in code, images or Git. Grant *:* or project Owner to apps. Share one role across unrelated services.

Lock it in

Badges, not master keys. Temporary passes, not copied keys.

Principal + action + resource + condition. Explicit deny wins, default deny. Workloads use roles/service accounts with short-lived credentials.

Interview questions

How does an app on EC2/EKS get AWS permissions without access keys?

EC2: an instance profile attaches a role; the SDK fetches temporary credentials from the instance metadata service (IMDSv2) and refreshes them. EKS: Pod Identity or IRSA maps a Kubernetes service account to an IAM role, giving each pod its own temporary credentials. No keys stored anywhere.

Identity-based vs resource-based policies?

Identity-based policies attach to a user/role and say what it can do. Resource-based policies attach to a resource (S3 bucket policy, SQS queue policy, KMS key policy) and say who can access it, including other accounts. Cross-account access usually needs both sides to allow.

Next: VPC networking →
04Foundations

VPC networking: subnets, routes, NAT and firewalls

A VPC is your private network in the cloud. Public subnets face the internet through an internet gateway; private subnets reach out through NAT; security groups decide which traffic each resource accepts.

In the food court

Ramu's section is fenced off (VPC). The serving counter faces the public hall (public subnet). The kitchen and storeroom are at the back with no public door (private subnets); staff can still go out to buy supplies through a back gate that only opens outward (NAT gateway). Each room has its own bouncer with a guest list (security group).

CIDR in 30 seconds

10.0.0.0/16 means "the first 16 bits are fixed": 216 = 65,536 addresses. A /24 has 256. Each extra bit halves the block. AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet.

LiveCIDR calculator: how many addresses, which range?
Security group (AWS) / firewall rule (GCP)Network ACL (AWS)
Applies toan instance / ENI (GCP: by network tags or service accounts)a whole subnet
Statestateful: replies are allowed automaticallystateless: allow both directions explicitly
Rulesallow only; can reference other security groupsallow and deny, numbered order
Typical use"DB accepts 5432 only from the app SG"coarse subnet blocks, rarely needed
VPC peering / Transit Gateway
Connect VPCs

Peering is 1:1 and non-transitive; Transit Gateway (or GCP Network Connectivity Center / Shared VPC) is a hub for many.

VPC endpoints / Private Service Connect
Reach cloud services privately

Call S3, DynamoDB or other APIs without going through NAT or the internet: cheaper and safer.

VPN / Direct Connect / Interconnect
Connect to an office or data centre

Encrypted tunnels over the internet, or dedicated private links.

Lock it in

Counter faces the hall, kitchen at the back, a back gate that only opens outward.

Public subnet = route to IGW; private = route to NAT. Only the load balancer is public. Security groups are stateful, NACLs stateless. Two AZs minimum.

Interview questions

What makes a subnet public?

Its route table has a route for 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway (and resources have public IPs). Private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway (outbound only) or have no internet route at all.

An app in a private subnet can't reach a third-party API. What do you check?

The subnet's route table (0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway in a public subnet, and that NAT's subnet routes to the IGW), the security group's outbound rules, the NACL in both directions (stateless, including ephemeral ports), DNS resolution, and whether the third party allow-lists your NAT's elastic IP.

05Running code

Compute and autoscaling: VMs that grow and shrink with demand

Pick an instance type for the workload, run several copies behind a load balancer, and let an autoscaling group keep a metric (like CPU) near a target.

In the food court

On weekday afternoons Ramu runs 2 stoves; at 8 pm on Fridays, 10. He tells the food court: "keep each stove about 60% busy; light another if they're hotter, turn one off if they're idle; never fewer than 2, never more than 12." That rule is target-tracking autoscaling.

LiveTarget-tracking autoscaling: drag the traffic and watch instances follow
Instance family (AWS / GCP)BalanceGood for
General purpose (m7g, m7i / e2, n2, n4)CPU ≈ memorymost web services
Compute optimised (c7g / c3)more CPUCPU-heavy APIs, encoding
Memory optimised (r7g / m3)more RAMcaches, large JVM heaps, analytics
Burstable (t4g / e2-micro)CPU creditslow, spiky traffic, dev
ARM (Graviton "g" / Axion, Tau T2A)better price/performanceJava runs fine on ARM: often 20%+ cheaper
GPU (g5, p5 / a3, g2)acceleratorsML training/inference

Scaling policies

target tracking
Keep a metric near a value

"Average CPU 60%" or "1,000 requests per instance". Simplest and usually best.

step scaling
Bigger alarm, bigger step

+1 at 70% CPU, +3 at 90%.

scheduled
Known peaks

Scale up at 7:45 pm before the IPL match, down at midnight.

predictive
Learn from history

Forecast daily patterns and scale ahead of them.

Things that bite

Warm-up time: a JVM instance takes 30–90 s to boot and get fast; scale on leading metrics and keep headroom. Statefulness: instances must be stateless (sessions in Redis, files in S3) or scale-in loses data. Health checks: the load balancer must stop sending traffic before an instance is terminated (connection draining / deregistration delay). Downstream limits: 10× instances = 10× DB connections.

Lock it in

Keep each stove 60% busy, between 2 and 12 stoves.

Launch template + ASG/MIG + LB health checks + target tracking. Min ≥ 2 across AZs. Stateless instances. Spot for interruptible work.

Interview questions

Vertical vs horizontal scaling in the cloud?

Vertical: a bigger instance type (needs a restart, has a ceiling, single point of failure). Horizontal: more instances behind a load balancer with autoscaling (needs stateless design, gives availability). Databases often scale vertically first, then with read replicas and sharding.

How would you handle a known traffic spike, like a sale at 8 pm?

Scheduled scale-out ahead of time (instances warm, caches primed), raise max capacity, pre-warm or request LB capacity if needed, load-test beforehand, put a queue in front of non-urgent work, rate-limit and have a degraded mode. See the JioHotstar case study in the System Design book.

Managed relational databases: what you get

HA

scale reads

Cold store, drawer, accounts office.

S3 for files (presigned URLs, lifecycle rules, block public access). Multi-AZ for availability, read replicas for scale, PITR for mistakes. Pick DynamoDB when access is by key at huge scale.

Interview questions

Multi-AZ vs read replica?

Multi-AZ is a synchronous standby for automatic failover; it doesn't serve reads (except in some newer cluster deployments). A read replica is an asynchronous copy that serves reads and can be promoted manually; it may lag. Use both: Multi-AZ for availability, replicas for read scaling.

How do you let users upload large files?

The API authorises the user and returns a short-lived presigned URL (or POST policy); the client uploads directly to S3/GCS, using multipart upload for large files. An S3 event triggers processing (virus scan, thumbnails) asynchronously. The bucket stays private and blocks public access.

Getting traffic in: DNS, CDN and load balancers

DNS turns the name into an address, the CDN serves what it can from the edge, and the load balancer spreads the rest over healthy instances.

In the food court

A customer asks the information desk for "Ramu Chai" and is told "stall 42" (DNS). Bottled water and biscuits are sold at kiosks by every entrance so nobody walks all the way in (CDN). At stall 42, a host sends each customer to whichever counter is free and skips the one with a broken till (load balancer + health checks).

Interview questions

How do health checks and connection draining work during a deploy?

The LB probes each target's health endpoint; only healthy targets receive traffic. When an instance is being removed, it's deregistered: the LB stops sending new requests and waits (deregistration delay) for in-flight requests to finish while the app shuts down gracefully. Readiness probes play the same role in Kubernetes.

How do you invalidate CDN content after a deploy?

Prefer versioned filenames (app.3f9a1.js) with long max-age so new deploys reference new URLs and nothing needs purging; keep HTML short-lived. For emergencies use an invalidation (CloudFront invalidation / Cloud CDN cache invalidation), which can take minutes and may cost money.

Serverless and messaging: Lambda, Cloud Run, queues and events

Serverless runs your code only when something happens and bills per use; queues and topics connect pieces without them waiting on each other.

In the food court

A stove that lights itself when an order slip drops in and switches off when idle: you pay only for cooking time (serverless). The first order after a quiet hour waits a moment while it heats up (cold start). Order slips pile on a spike so the kitchen works at its own pace (queue); an announcement over the loudspeaker reaches every counter that cares (pub/sub).

Serverless = pay per use, scale to zero, cold starts. Queue = one consumer; topic = fan-out. At-least-once delivery → idempotent consumers, visibility timeouts, DLQs.

Interview questions

When would you not use Lambda?

Long-running work (over 15 minutes), steady high traffic (containers are cheaper), latency-critical paths that can't tolerate cold starts, heavy frameworks with slow startup, or when you need persistent connections or local state. Cloud Run/Fargate or Kubernetes fit better.

SQS standard vs FIFO?

Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO: strict ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing within a deduplication window, with lower throughput limits. Choose FIFO only when order truly matters (per account, per order).

09Delivery

Docker: package the app with everything it needs

An image is a read-only, layered package of your app plus its runtime; a container is a running, isolated instance of it. Same image in dev, CI and production.

In the food court

Ramu packs each dish in a sealed tiffin box with its own spices and cutlery, so it tastes the same in any kitchen. The packing instructions (Dockerfile) are written once; the packed tiffin (image) is stored in a cold room (registry); opening and serving one is a container. Many tiffins share one stove (the host kernel), unlike renting a whole kitchen per dish (VMs).

LivePractice terminal: the Docker commands you'll use daily
Lock it in

Packing instructions, a sealed tiffin, a cold room, serving.

Dockerfile → image (layers, cached) → registry → container. Multi-stage, small JRE base, layered jar, non-root, versioned tags, config via env vars, logs to stdout.

Interview questions

Container vs VM?

A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor: strong isolation, GBs, minutes to boot. A container is an isolated process sharing the host's kernel (namespaces for isolation, cgroups for limits): MBs, starts in seconds, denser packing. Containers usually run on cloud VMs.

How do you make Docker builds fast and images small?

Order layers from least to most frequently changing (dependencies before source), multi-stage builds so build tools don't ship, slim/distroless or JRE base images, .dockerignore, Spring Boot layered jars or buildpacks, BuildKit cache mounts in CI, and scan images for vulnerabilities.

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments (or the default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT) and is replaced by arguments to docker run. Use the exec (JSON array) form so the process is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.

Kubernetes essentials

You declare the desired state in YAML ("3 copies of orders:1.4.0, healthy, behind a stable address"); Kubernetes' control loops keep reality matching it.

In the food court

Ramu hands the floor manager a card: "always have 3 counters serving masala chai from recipe v1.4". The manager places counters where there's space (scheduling), replaces any counter that collapses (self-healing), puts up one signboard that sends customers to whichever counters exist right now (Service), and when the card changes to v1.5, swaps counters one at a time so serving never stops (rolling update).

LivePractice terminal: kubectl for day-to-day work and debugging
Common failures and their meaning

ImagePullBackOff: wrong image name/tag or no registry permission. CrashLoopBackOff: the app exits on start (config, missing secret, OOM). Pending: no node has the requested CPU/memory. Pod running but no traffic: readiness probe failing or Service selector doesn't match labels. Restarts under load: liveness probe too strict (checking the DB from liveness is a classic mistake).

Lock it in

A card for the floor manager; he keeps the counters matching it.

Pod → Deployment → Service → Ingress. Requests/limits, startup/readiness/liveness probes, HPA, graceful shutdown. Declarative YAML in Git.

Interview questions

What happens when you run kubectl apply for a Deployment?

The API server authenticates/authorises and validates the object and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller creates/updates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects; the scheduler assigns each pod to a node with enough resources; that node's kubelet pulls the image and starts containers; probes mark them ready; endpoints are updated so the Service routes traffic to them.

Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes?

Startup: holds off the other probes until the app has booted (slow JVM start). Readiness: whether the pod should receive traffic; failing removes it from Service endpoints without restart. Liveness: whether the container is stuck and must be restarted; keep it to the process's own health.

Requests vs limits?

Requests are what the scheduler reserves and guarantees (placement and HPA utilisation are based on them). Limits are hard caps: CPU over the limit is throttled; memory over the limit gets the container OOMKilled. A common practice is memory request = limit, CPU limit unset or generous.

11Delivery

Where to run containers: ECS, Fargate, EKS, GKE or Cloud Run

Same container, different amounts of platform you manage. Choose the simplest option that meets your needs.

In the food court

Ramu can hand his tiffins to the food court's own serving service and never see a stove (Cloud Run, Fargate), or hire a floor manager and run his own counters with full control (EKS/GKE). The first is easier; the second is more flexible.

Cloud RunECS on FargateGKE AutopilotEKS / GKE Standard
You manageimage + a few settingstask definitions, servicesKubernetes objectsKubernetes + node groups/upgrades
Scale to zeroyesnono (pods)no
Kubernetes APIno (Knative-style)noyesyes
Billingper request/instance timeper task vCPU/GB-secondper pod resource requestsper node (VM)
Good forAPIs, small teams, bursty trafficAWS shops wanting simple containersKubernetes without node opsmany services, custom networking, operators, GPUs
Interview answer

"For a handful of stateless services I'd start on Cloud Run or ECS Fargate: no cluster to patch, autoscaling built in. Once we have many services, need service mesh, custom operators, GPUs or portability across clouds, a managed Kubernetes (EKS or GKE Autopilot) pays for its complexity."

Lock it in

The food court's serving service, or your own floor manager.

Cloud Run ≈ Fargate (serverless containers) < GKE Autopilot < EKS/GKE Standard in control and operational effort.

Interview questions

ECS vs EKS?

ECS is AWS's own simpler orchestrator tightly integrated with AWS (IAM per task, ALB, CloudWatch); EKS is managed Kubernetes with the full open ecosystem (Helm, operators, portability) but more concepts and upgrades to manage. Both run on EC2 nodes or Fargate.

Next: CI/CD and deployment strategies →
12Delivery

CI/CD and deployment strategies

CI: every commit is built and tested automatically. CD: every green build can be released safely, with a strategy that limits blast radius and allows instant rollback.

In the food court

A new recipe travels on a conveyor belt: tasted by the quality team (tests), sealed (image), first served at one counter to a few customers (canary), watched for complaints (metrics), then rolled out to every counter. If customers frown, the belt reverses (rollback).

LiveDeployment strategies: roll out v2 and inject a bug
StrategyHowProsCons
Recreatestop all v1, start v2simple, no mixed versionsdowntime
Rollingreplace pods a few at a timeno downtime, no extra capacity (Kubernetes default)v1 and v2 serve together; rollback is another roll
Blue-greenfull v2 stack beside v1; switch traffic at onceinstant switch and rollback, test v2 before switchingdouble capacity during deploy
Canarysend 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% to v2 while watching metricssmallest blast radius, data-drivenneeds good metrics and traffic splitting
Feature flagsdeploy dark, enable per user/percentage at runtimedecouples deploy from release, instant kill switchflag debt, testing combinations
Lock it in

Taste, seal, serve one counter, watch, then everyone.

CI on every commit; immutable images tagged by commit SHA; OIDC instead of stored keys; staging gates; canary or blue-green with automatic rollback on bad metrics; database migrations backward compatible.

Interview questions

Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?

Continuous delivery: every change is automatically built, tested and ready to release; production release is a button press (manual approval). Continuous deployment: every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically.

How do you deploy a database schema change without downtime?

Expand–migrate–contract: first deploy a backward-compatible change (add nullable column/new table) that both old and new app versions tolerate; deploy the app that writes both/reads new; backfill data; once no old version runs, remove the old column in a later release. Never rename or drop in the same release as the code change.

What is GitOps?

The desired state of every environment lives in Git (Kubernetes manifests, Helm values). An agent in the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) continuously syncs the cluster to Git. Deploys and rollbacks are pull requests and reverts, with history and review built in; the CI system needs no cluster credentials.

Next: Infrastructure as code with Terraform →
13Delivery

Infrastructure as code with Terraform

Describe your infrastructure in code, review it like code, and let the tool work out what to create, change or destroy. plan shows the diff; apply makes it real.

In the food court

Instead of telling workers "put a counter here, a fridge there" every time he opens a branch, Ramu keeps a blueprint in a drawer. For a new branch, the builders read the blueprint and build exactly that; if someone moved a fridge, the next inspection spots the drift and moves it back.

LivePractice terminal: the Terraform workflow
modules
Reuse

A "service" module (bucket + DB + IAM role) instantiated per environment with different variables.

state
Remote and locked

S3/GCS backend with locking; one state per environment/component to limit blast radius.

alternatives
Others

OpenTofu (open-source Terraform fork), Pulumi (real programming languages), CloudFormation/CDK (AWS only), Crossplane (Kubernetes-native).

Lock it in

A blueprint in a drawer; inspections spot drift.

Declarative code → init, plan (review), apply. Remote locked state, modules, no console clicking in prod, plans reviewed in PRs.

Interview questions

What is Terraform state and why does it matter?

A file mapping resources in code to real infrastructure IDs and attributes. Terraform uses it to compute plans. It must be shared (remote backend) and locked so two applies don't corrupt it, and protected because it can contain secrets. Losing it means Terraform no longer knows what it manages (recover with import).

Declarative vs imperative infrastructure?

Declarative: describe the end state (Terraform, Kubernetes YAML); the tool computes the steps and is idempotent. Imperative: a script of steps (CLI commands); re-running may create duplicates or fail. Declarative tools detect and correct drift.

In the food court

Opening day for Ramu's new orders counter: recipe tested, tiffins packed, the floor manager briefed, the counter behind the food court's main entrance, the cash box in the safe, a status board by the door. Here's the whole checklist.

Interview questions

Design the deployment of a Spring Boot REST API on AWS with high availability.

Route 53 + CloudFront/WAF → ALB in public subnets of two or three AZs → containers on ECS Fargate or EKS in private subnets (min 3 tasks across AZs, autoscaling on CPU/RPS, health checks on readiness) → RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ with a read replica and PITR, ElastiCache Redis, S3 for files. Secrets in Secrets Manager accessed via task/pod role. CI/CD with OIDC, image scanning, canary deploys. CloudWatch/Prometheus metrics, alarms on 5xx rate and latency, centralised logs, tracing. All defined in Terraform; separate prod account.

Operating in production: observe, secure, and pay less

Shipping is half the job. Knowing when it breaks, keeping attackers out, and not getting a surprise bill are the other half.

Observability, SLOs and alertingCloud security essentialsCost optimisation (FinOps)
15Operate

Observability, SLOs and alerting

Metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, logs tell you why. Alert on what users feel (SLOs), not on every CPU spike.

In the food court

Ramu doesn't stand at every counter. He watches a wall of gauges (metrics), follows a tracking number through every station when an order is late (traces), and reads the kitchen diary for that order (logs). His promise to customers: "99.5% of orders served within 5 minutes" (SLO). He only gets a phone call when that promise is at risk.

SignalAnswersAWSGCPOpen source
Metricshow much / how fast / how many errorsCloudWatch Metrics, Managed PrometheusCloud Monitoring, Managed PrometheusPrometheus + Grafana
Logswhat exactly happenedCloudWatch LogsCloud LoggingLoki, ELK/OpenSearch
Traceswhere the time went across servicesX-Ray / CloudWatch Application SignalsCloud TraceOpenTelemetry + Tempo/Jaeger
RED (services)
Rate, Errors, Duration

Requests per second, error rate, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) per endpoint.

USE (resources)
Utilisation, Saturation, Errors

CPU, memory, disk, connection pools, queue depth.

Golden signals
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation

Google SRE's four signals; same idea.

SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets

TermMeaningExample
SLI (indicator)a measurement of user experience% of requests answered successfully in < 300 ms
SLO (objective)the target for the SLI over a window99.9% over 30 days
Error budgetallowed failure: 100% − SLO0.1% ≈ 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days
SLA (agreement)a contractual promise with penalties, looser than the SLO99.5% or service credits
AvailabilityDowntime per yearper 30 days
99%3.65 days7.2 hours
99.9%8.76 hours43.2 minutes
99.95%4.38 hours21.6 minutes
99.99%52.6 minutes4.3 minutes
Good alerts

Page on symptoms: SLO burn rate (errors eating the budget fast), p99 latency above target, no successful orders in 5 minutes. Every alert has a runbook link.

Bad alerts

Page on causes that may not hurt users: one instance at 90% CPU, a single 500, disk at 70%. Those belong on dashboards or tickets.

Lock it in

Gauges, a tracking number, a diary, and one promise.

Metrics → traces → logs. RED for services, USE for resources. SLO 99.9% = 43 min/month budget. Alert on burn rate, with runbooks.

Interview questions

Your API's p99 latency doubled after a deploy. How do you investigate?

Confirm on dashboards (which endpoints, all instances or some, correlated with the deploy). Compare traces before/after to find the slow span (DB query, downstream call, GC). Check saturation: connection pool waits, CPU throttling, GC pauses. Check logs for errors/timeouts. If user impact is significant, roll back first, then investigate in staging with the same load.

What's an error budget used for?

It balances reliability and velocity: while budget remains, teams ship features and take risks; when it's exhausted, they freeze risky changes and invest in reliability. It turns "how reliable?" into an agreed number.

16Operate

Cloud security essentials

Most cloud breaches are misconfigurations: public buckets, leaked keys, over-broad permissions. Defend in layers: identity, network, data, workload, detection.

In the food court

Ramu's security isn't one big lock. Staff badges (identity), fences and back gates (network), a safe for cash with its own key held by head office (encryption with KMS), the recipe vault nobody copies into notebooks (secrets manager), CCTV that records who opened what (audit logs), and a guard who turns away troublemakers at the gate (WAF).

ThreatControl
Public S3/GCS bucket leakBlock Public Access at account level / uniform bucket-level access + org policy; presigned URLs
Leaked access keysno long-lived keys: roles, OIDC federation; secret scanning in Git; rotate
Over-privileged serviceleast-privilege policies, IAM Access Analyzer / Recommender, separate roles per service
Data theft at restKMS encryption (default on S3/EBS/RDS), customer-managed keys for sensitive data, key policies
Snooping in transitTLS everywhere, including inside the VPC (mTLS with a mesh)
Web attacks (SQLi, bots, DDoS)WAF managed rules, rate limiting, Shield/Cloud Armor
Vulnerable imagesscan in CI and registry, minimal base images, regular rebuilds
Nobody noticedCloudTrail/Audit Logs to a separate locked account, GuardDuty/Security Command Center, alerting
Lock it in

Badges, fences, a safe, a vault, CCTV and a guard.

Defence in depth. No secrets in code; roles not keys; private by default; encrypt everything; log every API call.

Interview questions

How do you store and rotate database credentials for a service?

Keep them in Secrets Manager / Secret Manager, encrypted with KMS; grant only the service's role read access to that one secret; inject at runtime (External Secrets, Spring Cloud AWS/GCP, CSI driver); enable automatic rotation and make the app re-read or use short-lived IAM database authentication where supported. Never bake into images or env files in Git.

What is envelope encryption?

Data is encrypted with a data key; the data key is encrypted with a master key in KMS that never leaves KMS. You store the encrypted data key next to the data. Decrypting needs a KMS call (permission-checked and audited) to unwrap the data key. It scales to large data and lets you rotate/revoke the master key centrally.

Next: Cost optimisation (FinOps) →
17Operate

Cost optimisation: pay for what you actually use

Most cloud waste is idle or oversized resources, forgotten environments, and data transfer. Measure by team with tags, then right-size, commit, and automate.

In the food court

The first month's bill shocks Ramu: stoves left burning overnight in the test kitchen, a giant fridge holding one bottle of milk, and porters charging for every trip between buildings. He labels every appliance with the branch that uses it, switches off the test kitchen at night, buys smaller fridges, and signs a yearly contract for the stoves he always needs.

1 · see
Visibility

Tag everything (team, service, env); Cost Explorer / Billing reports; budgets and anomaly alerts.

2 · cut waste
Idle and orphaned

Unattached disks, old snapshots, idle load balancers, dev environments running at night (schedule them off), unused Elastic IPs.

3 · right-size
Fit the workload

Use utilisation data (Compute Optimizer / Recommender); Kubernetes requests that match reality; ARM (Graviton/Axion) instances.

4 · commit
Discounts

Savings Plans / committed-use discounts for the steady baseline; spot for interruptible work.

5 · architecture
Design for cost

Cache to cut DB size, S3 lifecycle tiers, VPC endpoints instead of NAT for S3 traffic, keep chatty services in one AZ/region, serverless for low traffic.

Hidden bills

NAT gateway data processing (pulling images and calling S3 through NAT), cross-AZ and internet egress, CloudWatch log ingestion from verbose DEBUG logs, high-cardinality custom metrics, provisioned IOPS you don't use, and forgotten snapshots.

Lock it in

Label, switch off, shrink, sign a contract for the basics.

Tag → find waste → right-size → commit (Savings Plans) → spot → design for cost. Watch data transfer and logs.

Interview questions

Your AWS bill jumped 40% this month. What do you do?

Break down by service, account and tag in Cost Explorer to find the driver; check anomalies (new resources, data transfer, NAT, logs); identify the owner via tags; fix the cause (scale down, lifecycle rules, endpoints, log levels). Then prevent: budgets with alerts, anomaly detection, tagging policies, and cost reviews in the team's routine.

Linux I: navigating, files, permissions and text processing

Everything is a file, every file has an owner and permissions, and small commands joined with pipes do big jobs.

In the food court

The kitchen machines don't have buttons; you talk to them. "Go to the storeroom" (cd), "what's on this shelf?" (ls), "read me this label" (cat), "find every jar with 'chilli' on it" (grep). And every cupboard has a lock that says who may open, change, or use it (permissions).

2>&1send errors to the same place as output./run.sh > out.log 2>&1

Lock it in

Where am I, what's here, read it, find it, lock it.

pwd ls cd cat less head tail cp mv rm mkdir find grep · chmod 4-2-1 per owner/group/others · pipes: cut sort uniq awk sed wc.

Interview questions

Find the 10 most frequent errors in a log file.

grep ERROR app.log | awk -F'ERROR' '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10: filter error lines, keep the message part, sort so duplicates are adjacent, count, sort by count descending, top 10.

What does chmod 644 mean? 755?

644: owner read/write, group and others read only (typical files). 755: owner full, group and others read and execute (typical directories and scripts).

Linux II: processes, networking, services, logs and troubleshooting

When a server misbehaves: check load and memory, find the process, read its logs, test the network, check the disk. These commands cover 90% of incidents.

In the food court

A counter is slow. Ramu checks how busy every cook is (top), finds the one stuck (ps), reads the kitchen diary (journalctl), checks the phone line to the supplier (curl, dig), and looks at whether the storeroom is full (df).

LivePractice terminal: the "server is slow" runbook
TaskCommands
Processesps aux, top/htop, pgrep, kill -15 / -9, nice, jobs, fg/bg
Services and logssystemctl start|stop|restart|status|enable, journalctl -u svc -f, tail -f file, /var/log
Memory and CPUfree -h, uptime, nproc, vmstat 1, iostat
Diskdf -h, du -sh, lsblk, mount, lsof +L1 (deleted but open files)
Networkip a, ss -tulpn, curl -v, dig, ping, traceroute/mtr, nc -zv, tcpdump
Users and accesswhoami, id, sudo, useradd, passwd, ssh, scp/rsync

Lock it in

How busy, who's stuck, what does the diary say, is the line up, is the store full?

uptime top free ps → journalctl / tail -f → ss curl dig nc → df du. SIGTERM before SIGKILL. Services via systemd.

Interview questions

A Linux server is slow. Walk through your first five minutes.

uptime (load vs cores), top/htop (which process, user vs I/O wait), free -h (memory, swap), df -h (full disks), iostat/vmstat (disk and CPU saturation), the service's logs (journalctl), network checks (ss, curl to dependencies). For Java, thread dumps and GC stats. Compare with metrics history to see when it started.

df shows the disk full but du can't find the big files. Why?

A process still has a deleted file open (often a log deleted instead of rotated); the space isn't freed until the file descriptor closes. Find it with lsof +L1 and restart that process or truncate via /proc/PID/fd. Use logrotate with copytruncate or proper reopen signals.

SIGTERM vs SIGKILL?

SIGTERM (15) asks the process to exit; it can catch it and clean up (Spring Boot graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests). SIGKILL (9) can't be caught: the kernel kills it immediately. Docker and Kubernetes send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then SIGKILL.
